summary: This standards-track document covers RSVP-TE path diversity using exclusion information communicated during LSP setup. A typical use is protection, where two LSPs should follow different paths to avoid single points of failure. It specifies how to ask that a new path avoid chosen elements.

eli5.summary: If you want two roads to your friend that never share a bridge, you tell the second trip which places to skip.

questions: how to make rsvp-te lsps take different paths

subtitle: Asking RSVP-TE to route a new LSP away from an existing one, even when you cannot see the existing path.

tldr.problem: Protection needs two LSPs on different paths, but the node signaling the second LSP often cannot see the first path's links or SRLGs, for example across domains or a UNI, so the exclusions from RFC 4874 cannot be built.
tldr.mechanism: Two new Diversity subobjects, for the XRO and the EXRS, name the reference path with an abstract identifier: client-based (tunnel fields), PCE-based (a Path Key) or network-based (a Path Affinity Set).
tldr.outcome: Nodes that compute paths exclude the referenced path and report failures with defined PathErr codes. The RFC updates RFC 4874.

today: RFC 8390 is a Proposed Standard from July 2018 and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It updates RFC 4874.

sections.title: Diversity Without Knowing the Path
sections.content:
Path diversity is a well-known operational need: diverse Label Switched Paths (LSPs) share no network resources, which greatly reduces the chance of failing together. A source that knows the full topology can compute diverse paths itself. RFC 4874 added the eXclude Route Object (XRO) and the Explicit Exclusion Route Subobject (EXRS) so that nodes and resources, such as addresses and Shared Risk Link Groups (SRLGs), can be excluded.

That only works if the signaling source knows the properties of the path to avoid. It does not when the path to avoid neither starts, ends nor passes through the source, or when the source knows the path exists but has incomplete information because of operator policy. Inter-domain networks and GMPLS overlay networks can impose such restrictions.

The RFC's main example is the GMPLS User-Network Interface (UNI) overlay model, where core nodes do path computation and do not expose core topology or LSP paths to edge nodes. Edge node EN2 then cannot build an XRO to avoid the SRLGs of the EN1 to EN3 LSP.
sections.eli5: You want a second route that avoids the first one, but nobody will show you the first route's map. So you just point at the first route by name and ask the helper to avoid it.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Identifier
sections.content:
Each reference LSP or route is identified by an abstract identifier. Which kind to use depends on the core network operator's deployment. The RFC defines three.

Client-initiated. The identifier is made of the tunnel sender address, tunnel endpoint address, Tunnel ID and Extended Tunnel ID from RFC 3209, and local policy may add the LSP ID. In the example, the EN1 to EN3 LSP and the EN2 to EN4 LSP each exclude the other. The core network SHOULD implement crankback signaling (RFC 4920), which is known to lead to slower setup and sometimes suboptimal paths.

PCE-allocated. A Path Key (RFC 5520, RFC 5553) stands in for a hidden path segment. In the two-domain example, node U replaces {U, V, W} in the recorded route with a Path Key, and the source can then signal the next LSP to exclude that Path Key.

Network-assigned. A Path Affinity Set (PAS) is a single abstract SRLG identifier associated with a path, such as "123". A core node reads it as meaning to exclude the core SRLGs of LSPs tagged with that value. The PAS is kept inside the core network and not shared with the overlay.
sections.eli5: You can point at the first trip by its ticket number (client), by a secret code from a trusted guide (PCE), or by a label the railway gave it (network).

sections.title: The Diversity XRO Subobject
sections.content:
There are IPv4 and IPv6 forms, with XRO Type 38 for IPv4 and 39 for IPv6. Both start with an L flag, the type, a Length, a DI Type, A-Flags, E-Flags and a reserved field, then the Diversity Identifier Source Address and a variable Diversity Identifier Value.

The L flag works as in RFC 4874: 0 means the diversity constraints MUST be satisfied, and 1 means they SHOULD be. DI Type is 1 for client-initiated, 2 for PCE-allocated and 3 for network-assigned.

Attribute flags describe exceptions: 0x01 destination node exception, 0x02 processing node exception, 0x04 penultimate node exception (useful when the destination is single homed) and 0x08 LSP ID to be ignored, for tunnel-level exclusion. Exclusion flags say what must differ: 0x01 SRLG, 0x02 node and 0x04 link; 0x08 is reserved.

The source address is the address of the node that assigned the identifier: the reference LSP's tunnel sender, the node that assigned the Path Key, or the node allocating the PAS. The value is tunnel fields for DI Type 1, a Path Key for type 2, or a 32-bit PAS identifier scoped by the source address for type 3.
sections.eli5: The note has a label saying how to find the other trip, plus a few switches: skip the same bridges, the same towns, or the same roads, with a few allowed exceptions.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
The same type values 38 and 39 are used for Diversity subobjects inside an EXRS, which RFC 4874 uses to exclude resources between two abstract nodes of an explicit route. RFC 4874 processing is unchanged. A node that does not recognise the subobject follows RFC 4874.

An XRO or EXRS MAY carry several Diversity subobjects, for example several Path Keys, but they MUST all have the same DI Type. Mixed types make the node return a PathErr "Routing Problem" (24) with sub-code "XRO/EXRS Too Complex" (68 or 69). A recognised subobject with an unsupported DI Type gets sub-code "Unsupported Diversity Identifier Type" (36).

With client-initiated identifiers, all nodes on the path SHOULD check the constraint and MAY start crankback on a violation. With PCE or PAS identifiers, only nodes that perform path computation SHOULD process the information.

If the L flag is not set, the path MUST be diverse. If no path is found, the node returns "Routing Problem" (24) with "Route blocked by Exclude Route" (67). If the excluded path is unknown, the node SHOULD ignore the subobject, proceed, and after sending the Resv return "Notify Error" (25) with "Route of XRO LSP identifier unknown" (14).

If the L flag is set, the node SHOULD find a diverse path, but if it cannot it signals along the closest suitable path and returns "Notify Error" (25) with "Failed to satisfy Exclude Route" (15).
sections.eli5: If the rule is strict and the helper cannot find a separate road, it says no. If the rule is only a wish, it picks the closest road and tells you it could not do better.

sections.title: Re-evaluation After Setup
sections.content:
If an excluded path later becomes known, or changes, the processing node MUST re-evaluate the constraints of the diverse LSP.

When the L flag was not set and the constraints are no longer met, the node MUST send a PathErr with "Routing Problem" (24) and "Route blocked by Exclude Route" (67), without the Path_State_Removed flag. The source SHOULD move the LSP to a path that meets the original constraints.

When the L flag was set, a lost constraint produces "Notify Error" (25) with "Failed to satisfy Exclude Route" (15), and the source MAY leave the LSP where it is. If a previously unmet constraint becomes satisfiable, the node MUST send "Notify Error" (25) with the new sub-code "Compliant path exists" (16), and the source MAY move the LSP.
sections.eli5: If the first trip changes its route later, the helper checks again and warns you if your two trips now share a bridge.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it adds no security issues beyond those in the documents it builds on, among them RFC 5920, RFC 2205, RFC 3209, RFC 3473, RFC 2747, RFC 4874, RFC 5520 and RFC 5553.

RFC 4874 notes that some administrative boundaries may remove the XRO for security reasons. If that happened to a Diversity subobject, the diversity request would be silently dropped and a diverse path would be unlikely. So Diversity subobjects MUST be retained in an XRO crossing an administrative boundary, even if other subobjects are removed, based on operator policy. Use of the subobjects rests on mutual agreement, and identities of network resources need not be shared.
sections.eli5: The note that says "avoid trip 123" must not be thrown away at the border, or the request would be forgotten. It reveals nothing about the roads themselves.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned the IPv4 Diversity and IPv6 Diversity subobjects the values 38 and 39 in both the EXCLUDE_ROUTE and the EXPLICIT_ROUTE registries. It also defined new RSVP error sub-codes.

Under "Routing Problem" (24) it added 36, "Unsupported Diversity Identifier Type". Under "Notify Error" (25) it added 14, "Route of XRO LSP identifier unknown", 15, "Failed to satisfy Exclude Route", and 16, "Compliant path exists".
sections.eli5: IANA wrote the new codes in the official list so every router uses the same numbers.

items.label: Client-Initiated Identifier
items.desc: Reference LSP named by tunnel sender, endpoint, Tunnel ID and Extended Tunnel ID.

items.label: PCE-Allocated Identifier
items.desc: Reference path named by a Path Key.

items.label: Network-Assigned Identifier
items.desc: Reference path named by a Path Affinity Set identifier.

items.label: Unsupported Diversity Identifier Type
items.desc: Subobject recognised but its DI Type is not supported.

items.label: Route blocked by Exclude Route
items.desc: No path meets a strict constraint, or a strict constraint stopped being met.

items.label: XRO/EXRS Too Complex
items.desc: Diversity subobjects of different DI Types in one XRO or EXRS.

items.label: Route of XRO LSP identifier unknown
items.desc: Excluded path is unknown to the processing node.

items.label: Failed to satisfy Exclude Route
items.desc: A soft constraint could not be met.

items.label: Compliant path exists
items.desc: A previously unmet soft constraint can now be met.
